---
title: "Predicting cell death severity from hand-crafted image features"
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
---

Date: 13/7/2026

## GOHREP

**Goal:**

Test how well a CDA's 0-6 severity score can be predicted from twelve
hand-crafted image features, and find which of those features carry the signal.

**Hypothesis:**

The features are summaries of colour, brightness, texture and lesion geometry
that a human rater plausibly uses, and each one rises with severity, so a simple
model over the twelve should recover the score far better than chance. But
because no single feature separates neighbouring scores (adjacent-class AUC
peaks at 0.68 in `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction`), the models are
expected to place a CDA in roughly the right region of the scale while failing
to pin the exact score.

**Rationale:**

The features are extracted in `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction` and
written to `data/features/cda_image_features.csv`. This analysis starts from that
table and does nothing but model it. Three model families are fitted so the
result is not an artefact of one inductive bias: k-NN (local, no assumed form), a
random forest (non-linear, interaction-capable) and proportional-odds ordinal
regression (linear, and the only one that uses the fact the scale is ordered).
Each is scored under the same source-grouped cross validation, compared against a
majority-class baseline and a single-feature threshold rule, and the winner is
attributed with Gini importance and SHAP.

## 2. Features, class balance and a leakage-safe cross-validation

All modelling uses a class-balanced dataset, every score downsampled to the
smallest class, so the abundant score-0 class cannot dominate. Because the classes
are equal, a majority-class guess scores 1/7 and exact accuracy equals balanced
accuracy. Accuracy is reported as exact (predicted = true), near-miss (within one
point) and balanced (mean of the per-class exact accuracies).

The input is one row per cropped CDA image, read from
`data/features/cda_image_features.csv`. Each feature is a scalar summary of the
raw crop computed with no per-image threshold tuning, defined in full by
`10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction`. The "CDA" is the segmented cell-death
region, the "leaf" is all non-black pixels, and "greenness" means G - R (green
minus red channel).

| Variable | Feature | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `cda_green` | mean greenness inside the CDA | segmentation |
| `cda_bright` | mean brightness inside the CDA | segmentation |
| `cda_green_sd` | greenness spread within the CDA | segmentation |
| `cda_bright_sd` | brightness spread within the CDA | segmentation |
| `green_gap` | CDA greenness minus healthy-leaf greenness | segmentation |
| `ent_gap` | CDA Shannon entropy minus healthy-leaf entropy | segmentation |
| `sep` | bimodality of the leaf-greenness distribution | segmentation |
| `leaf_green_sd` | greenness spread over the whole leaf | segmentation |
| `mean_green` | mean green-channel intensity over the leaf | `09_image_entropy` |
| `log_gr` | log green-pixel to red-pixel count ratio | `09_image_entropy` |
| `leaf_bright` | mean brightness over the leaf | `09_image_entropy` |
| `entropy_raw` | Shannon entropy of the raw crop | `09_image_entropy` |

Two further columns are not model features. `frac_g_gt_r` (CDA area over leaf
area) is used only for the single-feature baseline, since Otsu splits every leaf
whether or not a lesion is present, and `source` names the leaf each crop came
from and groups the folds below.

Crops from one leaf share lighting, plant and tissue, so they are not
independent. Whole leaves are therefore assigned to folds, and no leaf ever
appears in both the training and held-out folds.

- Balancing leaves 436 crops per class and 3052 in total, so the majority-class
  floor is 1/7 and exact accuracy equals balanced accuracy.
- A shuffled-label run returns 0.146 against a 0.143 chance level, so the
  pipeline carries no leakage of its own.

```{r}
# 2.1  Features and class balancing
# All twelve features (plus the area baseline and the source leaf) come from the
# table exported by 10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction.
features <- read.csv(here("data", "features", "cda_image_features.csv"))

seg_features <- c(
  "ent_gap", "green_gap", "cda_green", "sep",
  "cda_green_sd", "cda_bright", "cda_bright_sd", "leaf_green_sd",
  "mean_green", "log_gr", "leaf_bright"
)
other_features <- c("entropy_raw")
all_features <- c(seg_features, other_features)

# frac_g_gt_r is not a model feature (its Otsu-artefact behaviour is discussed in
# 10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction section 5.2); it is kept in the frame
# only for the single-feature "Threshold: CDA area" baseline in section 6.
feat_all <- features %>%
  select(image_id, source, score, frac_g_gt_r, all_of(all_features))

set.seed(42)
min_n <- min(table(feat_all$score))
bal_idx <- unlist(lapply(0:6, function(s) {
  idx <- which(feat_all$score == s)
  if (length(idx) > min_n) sample(idx, min_n) else idx
}))
feat <- feat_all[bal_idx, ]
X <- as.matrix(feat[, all_features])
y <- feat$score
cat(sprintf(
  "Balanced set: %d images per class, %d total, %d features\n",
  min_n, nrow(feat), length(all_features)
))
```

```{r}
# 2.2  Source-grouped 5-fold assignment (a leaf's crops never split across folds)
# `source` is the crop filename <SourceBasename>_<Row>_<Col>_<Pos> with the
# trailing _Row_Col_Pos stripped, i.e. the source leaf image.
K <- 5
set.seed(42)
usrc <- unique(feat$source)
src_fold <- setNames(sample(rep(1:K, length.out = length(usrc))), usrc)
fold <- unname(src_fold[feat$source])
cat(sprintf(
  "%d source leaves assigned across %d folds; fold sizes: %s\n",
  length(usrc), K, paste(as.integer(table(fold)), collapse = ", ")
))

metric_row <- function(pred, name, tuning = "") {
  per <- vapply(0:6, function(s) mean(pred[y == s] == s), numeric(1))
  data.frame(
    model = name, tuning = tuning,
    exact = mean(pred == y), near_miss = mean(abs(pred - y) <= 1),
    balanced = mean(per)
  )
}
# Per-fold accuracy, so the cross-validation is fully transparent (reported
# alongside the mean, not just pooled).
per_fold <- function(pred, name) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:K, function(f) {
    m <- fold == f
    data.frame(
      model = name, fold = as.character(f), n = sum(m),
      exact = mean(pred[m] == y[m]),
      near_miss = mean(abs(pred[m] - y[m]) <= 1)
    )
  }))
}
```

```{r}
# 2.3  Random-forest regressor under the grouped cross validation, plus a leakage sanity check.
rf_reg_cv <- function(ntree, target = y) {
  pred <- numeric(length(target))
  for (f in 1:K) {
    tr <- fold != f
    te <- fold == f
    m <- randomForest::randomForest(x = X[tr, , drop = FALSE], y = target[tr], ntree = ntree)
    pred[te] <- predict(m, X[te, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  pmin(pmax(round(pred), 0), 6)
}
# Shuffle the labels: a correctly-built cross validation with no leakage MUST collapse to chance.
set.seed(7)
y_shuffled <- sample(y)
shuffle_acc <- mean(rf_reg_cv(200, y_shuffled) == y_shuffled)
cat(sprintf(
  "Leakage check - shuffled-label cross validation exact accuracy = %.3f (chance = %.3f)\n",
  shuffle_acc, 1 / 7
))
```

---

## 3. Choosing k for k-NN

Only held-out accuracy is shown, since at k = 1 each training point is its own
neighbour and scores 100% by construction.

- Held-out accuracy climbs from 0.462 at k = 1 to 0.556 at k = 27, so single
  nearest neighbours overfit the local noise and averaging fixes it.
- Every k from 5 upward lands between 0.511 and 0.556, so the exact choice of k
  matters far less than the ceiling the feature space imposes.

```{r}
# 3.1
knn_cv <- function(ks) {
  P <- matrix(0L, nrow(X), length(ks), dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("k", ks)))
  for (f in 1:K) {
    tr <- fold != f
    te <- fold == f
    mu <- colMeans(X[tr, ])
    sdv <- apply(X[tr, ], 2, sd)
    sdv[sdv == 0] <- 1
    Xtr <- scale(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], mu, sdv)
    Xte <- scale(X[te, , drop = FALSE], mu, sdv)
    d <- outer(rowSums(Xte^2), rowSums(Xtr^2), "+") - 2 * Xte %*% t(Xtr)
    ytr <- y[tr]
    ord <- t(apply(d, 1, order))
    for (j in seq_along(ks)) {
      P[te, j] <- apply(ord[, 1:ks[j], drop = FALSE], 1, function(ix) {
        tb <- table(ytr[ix])
        as.integer(names(tb)[which.max(tb)])
      })
    }
  }
  P
}
kseq <- seq(1, 51, by = 2)
knn_preds <- knn_cv(kseq)
knn_curve <- data.frame(
  k = kseq,
  exact = apply(knn_preds, 2, function(p) mean(p == y)),
  near_miss = apply(knn_preds, 2, function(p) mean(abs(p - y) <= 1))
)
best_k <- kseq[which.max(knn_curve$exact)]
cat(sprintf(
  "Best k = %d  (held-out exact = %.3f, near-miss = %.3f)\n",
  best_k, max(knn_curve$exact), knn_curve$near_miss[knn_curve$k == best_k]
))
```

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
# 3.2
p_ksweep <- ggplot(knn_curve, aes(k, exact)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166AC") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2166AC", size = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_k, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(min(knn_curve$exact) - 0.02, max(knn_curve$exact) + 0.02)) +
  labs(
    x = "k (number of neighbours)", y = "Held-out exact accuracy (grouped 5-fold cross validation)",
    title = sprintf("k-NN: held-out accuracy is flat beyond k ~ 5; chosen k = %d", best_k)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 12), axis.title = element_text(size = 13))
p_ksweep
save_plot(p_ksweep, "seg_knn_k_sweep.png", width = 8, height = 4.5)
```

## 4. Random forest: regularising to control overfitting

The forest is fixed at 200 trees and tree size is capped with `maxnodes`, taking
the largest held-out accuracy whose train-to-held-out gap stays within 15 points.
Training accuracy is fit and scored on all the data, held-out is the grouped
5-fold cross validation.

- Capping trees at 128 leaf nodes reaches 0.562 held-out for a gap of 0.109,
  while 256 nodes adds only 0.010 held-out accuracy for a 0.168 gap that breaks
  the 15-point rule.
- Training accuracy keeps climbing (0.370 to 0.741 across the sweep, and 0.924
  fully grown) while held-out accuracy stalls near 0.57, so the extra capacity is
  memorisation rather than signal.

```{r}
# 4.1
NTREE <- 200
rf_fit_cv <- function(maxnodes) { # grouped cross validation (held-out) predictions
  pred <- numeric(length(y))
  for (f in 1:K) {
    tr <- fold != f
    te <- fold == f
    m <- randomForest::randomForest(
      x = X[tr, , drop = FALSE], y = y[tr],
      ntree = NTREE, maxnodes = maxnodes
    )
    pred[te] <- predict(m, X[te, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  pmin(pmax(round(pred), 0), 6)
}
rf_fit_train <- function(maxnodes) { # resubstitution (training) predictions
  set.seed(1)
  m <- randomForest::randomForest(x = X, y = y, ntree = NTREE, maxnodes = maxnodes)
  pmin(pmax(round(predict(m, X)), 0), 6)
}
maxnodes_grid <- c(4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256)
set.seed(42)
reg_curve <- data.frame(
  maxnodes = maxnodes_grid,
  train = sapply(maxnodes_grid, function(mn) mean(rf_fit_train(mn) == y)),
  cross_validation = sapply(maxnodes_grid, function(mn) mean(rf_fit_cv(mn) == y))
)
reg_curve$gap <- reg_curve$train - reg_curve$cross_validation
best_maxnodes <- max(reg_curve$maxnodes[reg_curve$gap <= 0.15])
cat(sprintf(
  "Chosen maxnodes = %d: train = %.3f, cross validation = %.3f, gap = %.3f (<= 0.15)\n",
  best_maxnodes,
  reg_curve$train[reg_curve$maxnodes == best_maxnodes],
  reg_curve$cross_validation[reg_curve$maxnodes == best_maxnodes],
  reg_curve$gap[reg_curve$maxnodes == best_maxnodes]
))
rf_best <- rf_fit_cv(best_maxnodes) # held-out predictions of the chosen model
```

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
# 4.2
p_reg <- reg_curve %>%
  pivot_longer(c(train, cross_validation), names_to = "set", values_to = "accuracy") %>%
  ggplot(aes(maxnodes, accuracy, colour = set)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_maxnodes, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(train = "#B2182B", cross_validation = "#2166AC"),
    labels = c(cross_validation = "held out (grouped 5-fold cross validation)", train = "training"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = maxnodes_grid) +
  labs(
    x = "max leaf nodes per tree (log scale)", y = "Exact accuracy",
    title = sprintf("RF regularisation: train-cross-validation gap kept <= 15%%; maxnodes = %d", best_maxnodes)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 12), axis.title = element_text(size = 13))
p_reg
save_plot(p_reg, "seg_rf_regularisation.png", width = 8, height = 4.5)
```

### 4.1 Does the tree count matter?

The 200 trees above are asserted rather than tuned, so the sweep is repeated
across tree counts. Unlike `maxnodes`, the number of trees is not a capacity
parameter. A random forest averages independently grown trees, and its
generalisation error converges as trees are added rather than degrading
(Breiman 2001), so more trees should buy variance reduction and nothing else.
If that holds, the table below is flat along its rows and the chosen `maxnodes`
does not depend on the tree count.

- Held-out accuracy climbs by up to 0.014 between 25 and 100 trees, then moves by
  at most 0.007 out to 800, against a 0.005 spread from merely re-seeding a
  single setting, so the plateau arrives by roughly 100 trees.
- The best cap is 256 leaf nodes in all six columns, so the two settings do not
  interact and the chosen `maxnodes` would be identical at any tree count.
- 200 trees therefore sits comfortably past the plateau, and a full
  two-dimensional search would cost six times the compute to return the same
  model.

```{r}
# 4.3  ntree x maxnodes, under the same undersample and grouped folds as above.
# Cached: the full grid is 42 cross-validated forests and takes a few minutes.
ntree_cache <- here(
  "analyses", "10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction", "model_cache",
  "ntree_sweep.rds"
)
if (file.exists(ntree_cache)) {
  nts <- readRDS(ntree_cache)
} else {
  rf_cv_at <- function(nt, mn) {
    pred <- numeric(length(y))
    for (f in 1:K) {
      tr <- fold != f
      te <- fold == f
      m <- randomForest::randomForest(
        x = X[tr, , drop = FALSE], y = y[tr], ntree = nt, maxnodes = mn
      )
      pred[te] <- predict(m, X[te, , drop = FALSE])
    }
    mean(pmin(pmax(round(pred), 0), 6) == y)
  }
  ntrees <- c(25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800)
  sweep <- matrix(NA_real_, length(maxnodes_grid), length(ntrees),
    dimnames = list(maxnodes_grid, ntrees)
  )
  for (i in seq_along(maxnodes_grid)) {
    for (j in seq_along(ntrees)) {
      set.seed(42)
      sweep[i, j] <- rf_cv_at(ntrees[j], maxnodes_grid[i])
    }
  }
  # Repeat one cell across seeds to size the run-to-run noise, so the table's
  # column-to-column differences can be judged against it.
  reruns <- sapply(1:5, function(s) {
    set.seed(s)
    rf_cv_at(200, 128)
  })
  nts <- list(sweep = sweep, ntrees = ntrees, maxnodes = maxnodes_grid, reruns = reruns)
  dir.create(dirname(ntree_cache), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  saveRDS(nts, ntree_cache)
}

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(maxnodes = nts$maxnodes, round(nts$sweep, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Held-out exact accuracy (grouped 5-fold). Columns are tree counts."
)
cat(sprintf(
  "Best maxnodes per tree count: %s\n",
  paste(unique(nts$maxnodes[apply(nts$sweep, 2, which.max)]), collapse = ", ")
))
cat(sprintf(
  "Re-running ntree = 200, maxnodes = 128 across 5 seeds: sd = %.4f, range = %.3f\n",
  sd(nts$reruns), diff(range(nts$reruns))
))
```

## 5. Ordinal regression

Proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression fits one linear predictor to the 12
features and six ordered cut-points that split it into the seven classes, so the
model uses the ordering of the scale rather than treating the classes as
unrelated labels. It has no hyperparameter, so there is no sweep.

- Held-out exact accuracy is 0.615 against 0.616 training, a gap of 0.002, so
  twelve coefficients plus six cut-points leave nothing to memorise.
- Near-miss accuracy is 0.978, so all but 2% of crops land within one point of
  the true score.

```{r}
# 5.1  Ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds, MASS::polr), scored under
# the same source-grouped cross validation. Features are standardised with
# training-fold statistics inside each fold, so nothing leaks into the scaling.
ord_cv <- function() {
  pred <- integer(length(y))
  for (f in 1:K) {
    tr <- fold != f
    te <- fold == f
    mu <- colMeans(X[tr, ])
    sdv <- apply(X[tr, ], 2, sd)
    sdv[sdv == 0] <- 1
    dtr <- data.frame(scale(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], mu, sdv),
      y = factor(y[tr], levels = 0:6, ordered = TRUE)
    )
    dte <- data.frame(scale(X[te, , drop = FALSE], mu, sdv))
    fit <- suppressWarnings(MASS::polr(y ~ ., data = dtr, Hess = TRUE))
    pred[te] <- as.integer(as.character(predict(fit, dte, type = "class")))
  }
  pred
}
ord_train <- function() {
  mu <- colMeans(X)
  sdv <- apply(X, 2, sd)
  sdv[sdv == 0] <- 1
  d <- data.frame(scale(X, mu, sdv), y = factor(y, levels = 0:6, ordered = TRUE))
  fit <- suppressWarnings(MASS::polr(y ~ ., data = d, Hess = TRUE))
  as.integer(as.character(predict(fit, data.frame(scale(X, mu, sdv)), type = "class")))
}
ord_best <- ord_cv()
ord_tr <- ord_train()
ord_fmt <- paste0(
  "Ordinal regression: held-out (grouped cross validation) exact = %.3f, near-miss = %.3f; ",
  "training = %.3f, gap = %.3f\n"
)
cat(sprintf(
  ord_fmt,
  mean(ord_best == y), mean(abs(ord_best - y) <= 1),
  mean(ord_tr == y), mean(ord_tr == y) - mean(ord_best == y)
))
```

### 5.1 Distribution over 1,000 undersamples

Every accuracy above rests on one balanced undersample drawn at seed 42, which
throws away 52% of the crops and could be lucky or unlucky. The whole experiment
is therefore repeated 1,000 times, each iteration drawing a fresh undersample of
436 crops per class and a fresh source-grouped fold assignment, then scoring the
ordinal regression exactly as above. Both accuracies are held-out: every crop is
predicted only while its leaf sits in the held-out fold, and the 3052 out-of-fold
predictions are pooled once all five folds are done. This mirrors the repeat stratified
undersampling used for the human scoring in `03_human_performance`, so the model
and the raters are summarised the same way.

- Across 1,000 undersamples exact accuracy averages 0.608 with a 95% interval of
  0.597 to 0.619, so which crops are drawn moves the headline by about a point in
  either direction.
- The seed-42 draw used above scores 0.615, the 91st percentile of that
  distribution, so the single figure quoted for it is mildly lucky rather than
  typical.
- Every one of the 1,000 draws still beats the random forest (0.565) and k-NN
  (0.556), and near-miss accuracy varies by only sd 0.0018, so both the model
  ranking and the one-point reliability survive resampling.

```{r}
# 5.2  1,000 undersamples, each scored by the same grouped 5-fold ordinal
# regression. Cached: the loop takes about 15 minutes.
ord_dist_cache <- here(
  "analyses", "10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction", "model_cache",
  "ordinal_undersample_dist.rds"
)
if (file.exists(ord_dist_cache)) {
  ord_dist <- readRDS(ord_dist_cache)
} else {
  # Seed i drives both the undersample and the fold assignment, so each
  # iteration is an independent repeat of the entire experiment.
  ord_once <- function(seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    b <- unlist(lapply(0:6, function(s) {
      idx <- which(feat_all$score == s)
      if (length(idx) > min_n) sample(idx, min_n) else idx
    }))
    f <- feat_all[b, ]
    Xi <- as.matrix(f[, all_features])
    yi <- f$score
    u <- unique(f$source)
    fo <- unname(setNames(sample(rep(1:K, length.out = length(u))), u)[f$source])
    pred <- integer(length(yi))
    for (k in 1:K) {
      tr <- fo != k
      te <- fo == k
      mu <- colMeans(Xi[tr, ])
      sdv <- apply(Xi[tr, ], 2, sd)
      sdv[sdv == 0] <- 1
      dtr <- data.frame(scale(Xi[tr, , drop = FALSE], mu, sdv),
        y = factor(yi[tr], levels = 0:6, ordered = TRUE)
      )
      fit <- suppressWarnings(MASS::polr(y ~ ., data = dtr, Hess = TRUE))
      pred[te] <- as.integer(as.character(
        predict(fit, data.frame(scale(Xi[te, , drop = FALSE], mu, sdv)), type = "class")
      ))
    }
    c(exact = mean(pred == yi), near_miss = mean(abs(pred - yi) <= 1))
  }
  res <- vapply(seq_len(1000), ord_once, numeric(2))
  ord_dist <- data.frame(
    iteration = seq_len(1000), exact = res["exact", ], near_miss = res["near_miss", ]
  )
  dir.create(dirname(ord_dist_cache), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  saveRDS(ord_dist, ord_dist_cache)
}

ord_summary <- function(v) {
  sprintf(
    "mean = %.3f, sd = %.4f, 95%% interval [%.3f, %.3f]",
    mean(v), sd(v), quantile(v, 0.025), quantile(v, 0.975)
  )
}
cat(sprintf("Exact      : %s\n", ord_summary(ord_dist$exact)))
cat(sprintf("Near-miss  : %s\n", ord_summary(ord_dist$near_miss)))
cat(sprintf(
  "Seed-42 undersample sits at the %.0fth percentile of the exact distribution.\n",
  100 * mean(ord_dist$exact <= mean(ord_best == y))
))
```

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
# 5.3  Histograms matching 03_human_performance's distribution plots: sky-blue
# bars with a dashed red mean line (red is kept for the mean so it cannot be
# confused with the bars).
#
# Every iteration scores the same 3052 held-out predictions, so an accuracy can
# only ever be an integer multiple of 1/3052. Bins that are not a whole number of
# those steps wide therefore capture 3 attainable values in one bar and 2 in the
# next, leaving a comb of empty gaps that is an artefact of the binning rather
# than of the distribution. Bin width is fixed to `m` whole steps and the edges
# are offset by half a step, so each bar covers exactly m attainable values.
n_pred <- nrow(feat)
dist_panel <- function(v, xlab, title, target_bins = 20) {
  step <- 1 / n_pred
  m <- max(1, round(diff(range(v)) / (target_bins * step)))
  ggplot(data.frame(v = v), aes(v)) +
    geom_histogram(
      binwidth = m * step, boundary = min(v) - step / 2,
      fill = "skyblue", colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_vline(
      xintercept = mean(v), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    labs(
      x = xlab, y = "Frequency",
      title = sprintf("%s (mean %.3f)", title, mean(v))
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11), axis.title = element_text(size = 12))
}
p_dist <- dist_panel(ord_dist$exact, "Held-out exact accuracy", "Exact") |
  dist_panel(ord_dist$near_miss, "Held-out near-miss accuracy", "Near-miss")
p_dist
save_plot(p_dist, "seg_ordinal_undersample_dist.png", width = 10, height = 4.5)
```

## 6. Model comparison, with per-fold results

- Ordinal regression leads at 0.615 held-out against 0.565 for the random forest
  and 0.556 for k-NN, so the linear model that uses the ordering of the scale
  beats both models that do not.
- The single-feature CDA-area rule reaches 0.111, below the 0.143 majority-class
  floor, confirming that lesion area carries no usable severity signal on its own.

```{r}
# 6.1
# Held-out (grouped cross validation) predictors. The ordinal-regression
# predictors (ord_best, ord_tr) are defined in section 5 above.
thresh_cv <- function(x) {
  pred <- integer(length(y))
  for (f in 1:K) {
    tr <- fold != f
    te <- fold == f
    med <- tapply(x[tr], y[tr], median)
    sc <- as.integer(names(med))
    o <- order(sc)
    med <- med[o]
    sc <- sc[o]
    cuts <- cummax((head(med, -1) + tail(med, -1)) / 2)
    pred[te] <- sc[findInterval(x[te], cuts) + 1]
  }
  pred
}
# Training (resubstitution) predictors, for the train-cross-validation gap
thresh_train <- function(x) {
  med <- tapply(x, y, median)
  sc <- as.integer(names(med))
  o <- order(sc)
  med <- med[o]
  sc <- sc[o]
  cuts <- cummax((head(med, -1) + tail(med, -1)) / 2)
  sc[findInterval(x, cuts) + 1]
}
knn_train_at <- function(k) { # self-inclusive; meaningful for k > 1
  mu <- colMeans(X)
  sdv <- apply(X, 2, sd)
  sdv[sdv == 0] <- 1
  Xs <- scale(X, mu, sdv)
  d <- outer(rowSums(Xs^2), rowSums(Xs^2), "+") - 2 * Xs %*% t(Xs)
  ord <- t(apply(d, 1, order))
  apply(ord[, 1:k, drop = FALSE], 1, function(ix) {
    tb <- table(y[ix])
    as.integer(names(tb)[which.max(tb)])
  })
}

knn_best <- knn_preds[, which(kseq == best_k)]
maj <- rep(as.integer(names(which.max(table(y)))), length(y))

cmp_row <- function(train_pred, test_pred, name, tuning) {
  data.frame(
    model = name, tuning = tuning,
    train = mean(train_pred == y), cross_validation = mean(test_pred == y),
    gap = mean(train_pred == y) - mean(test_pred == y),
    near_miss = mean(abs(test_pred - y) <= 1)
  )
}
results <- rbind(
  cmp_row(maj, maj, "Majority class", ""),
  cmp_row(thresh_train(feat$frac_g_gt_r), thresh_cv(feat$frac_g_gt_r), "Threshold: CDA area", "1 feature"),
  cmp_row(ord_tr, ord_best, "Ordinal regression", "12 features"),
  cmp_row(knn_train_at(best_k), knn_best, "k-NN", sprintf("k = %d", best_k)),
  cmp_row(rf_fit_train(best_maxnodes), rf_best, "Random forest", sprintf("%d nodes", best_maxnodes))
)

results %>%
  mutate(across(c(train, cross_validation, gap, near_miss), ~ round(., 3)),
    overfit = ifelse(gap > 0.15, "DISCARD", "ok")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cross_validation)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

```{r}
# 6.2  Per-fold breakdown of the best model (chosen by held-out accuracy).
cv_preds <- list("Random forest" = rf_best, "k-NN" = knn_best, "Ordinal regression" = ord_best)
best_cv_name <- names(cv_preds)[which.max(vapply(cv_preds, function(p) mean(p == y), numeric(1)))]
pf <- per_fold(cv_preds[[best_cv_name]], best_cv_name)
print(transform(pf, exact = round(exact, 3), near_miss = round(near_miss, 3)))
cat(sprintf(
  "MEAN across folds: exact = %.3f (fold range %.3f-%.3f); near-miss = %.3f\n",
  mean(pf$exact), min(pf$exact), max(pf$exact), mean(pf$near_miss)
))
```

- Per-fold exact accuracy spans 0.592 to 0.634 across the five folds, so the
  headline 0.615 is not the product of one lucky split.
- For reference, and not a like-for-like comparison, the project's deep-learning
  models reach 60-67% held-out test accuracy against 61.5% here, so twelve
  hand-crafted features land in the same range as a learned representation.

## 7. Confusion matrix of the best model

Everything from here on is fitted on the single seed-42 undersample used
throughout, not on any of the 1,000 draws above and not on the best of them.
Picking the best draw would select the top of a distribution and bias every
figure downstream, but the fixed draw is not neutral either: it reports 61.5%
exact against a resampled mean of 60.8%, so the percentages below sit at the
optimistic end by roughly a point.

- Errors are almost all off-by-one: 36.3% of crops land exactly one class away
  and only 2.2% two or more, which is the tight band diagonal.
- The ends of the scale are recovered best (79.8% at score 0 and 71.1% at score
  6) while every interior class sits near 55%, so the middle of the scale is
  where the features run out.

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
# 7.1
model_preds <- list(
  "Random forest" = rf_best, "k-NN" = knn_best,
  "Ordinal regression" = ord_best
)
best_name <- names(model_preds)[which.max(vapply(
  model_preds,
  function(p) mean(p == y), numeric(1)
))]
best_pred <- model_preds[[best_name]]

cm <- as.data.frame(table(true = factor(y, 0:6), pred = factor(best_pred, 0:6)))
p_cm <- ggplot(cm, aes(x = pred, y = true, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey90") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#B2182B", guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted score", y = "True score",
    title = sprintf(
      "%s (grouped cross validation): exact %.1f%%, near-miss %.1f%%",
      best_name, 100 * mean(best_pred == y),
      100 * mean(abs(best_pred - y) <= 1)
    )
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12), axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12), panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
p_cm
save_plot(p_cm, "seg_confusion_matrix.png", width = 7, height = 6)
```

  greenness variation last at 37, so lesion colour dominates the splits.
- The top five span only 234 to 139 and several of them are near duplicates, so
  the ranking should be read as blocks rather than a strict per-feature order.

## 9. SHAP analysis

Gini importance is global and directionless. SHAP attributes each prediction to
its features, showing magnitude and direction, computed here on the random forest
regressor with an interventional, class-balanced background set.

- The log green-to-red ratio and CDA greenness dominate, and high values of both
  push the prediction upward across the whole explanation set, so the model reads
  severity mainly off lesion colour.
- The four weakest features stay within 0.05 of zero, and within-CDA greenness
  variation contributes a mean absolute SHAP of 0.01, so lesion mottling barely
  moves a prediction.

```{r}
#| output: false
# 9.1
library(kernelshap)
library(shapviz)

set.seed(1)
rf_reg <- randomForest::randomForest(x = X, y = y, ntree = NTREE, maxnodes = best_maxnodes)

# Class-balanced background (~14/class) and a class-balanced explanation set.
Xdf <- as.data.frame(X)
bg_idx <- unlist(lapply(0:6, function(s) sample(which(y == s), 14)))
ex_idx <- unlist(lapply(0:6, function(s) sample(which(y == s), 20)))
shp <- shapviz(suppressWarnings(
  permshap(rf_reg, X = Xdf[ex_idx, ], bg_X = Xdf[bg_idx, ])
))
y_ex <- y[ex_idx]
```

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
# 9.2 Beeswarm: global importance + direction of each feature's effect.
p_bee <- sv_importance(shp, kind = "beeswarm", max_display = length(all_features)) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11))
p_bee
save_plot(p_bee, "seg_shap_beeswarm.png", width = 8, height = 6)
```

- All three leading features have monotonic effects, but CDA brightness is flat
  below about 100 and only then climbs from -0.25 to +0.6, so once a lesion is
  dark enough the model stops distinguishing further dimming.
- The log green-to-red ratio saturates at both ends, sitting near -0.7 below -8
  and near +0.5 above 0, so extreme values add nothing beyond the threshold.

```{r fig.width=11, fig.height=4}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
# 9.3 Dependence plots for the three most important features (by mean |SHAP|).
mean_abs <- sort(colMeans(abs(get_shap_values(shp))), decreasing = TRUE)
top3 <- names(mean_abs)[1:3]
p_dep <- patchwork::wrap_plots(lapply(top3, function(v) {
  sv_dependence(shp, v = v, color_var = NULL) + theme_minimal()
}), nrow = 1)
p_dep
save_plot(p_dep, "seg_shap_dependence.png", width = 11, height = 4)
```

- The top two features are the same at both ends of the scale, so the model is
  not running on separate low- and high-severity specialists.
- Greenness bimodality matters more at low severity (0.30 against 0.19) while CDA
  brightness rises from fifth to third, which fits bimodality's role in telling a
  faint lesion from none at all.

```{r}
# 9.4 Does the feature ranking reshuffle between low (0-1) and high (5-6)
# severity? (mean |SHAP| per feature, matching the AutoCDAScorer MSHAP table.)
S <- abs(get_shap_values(shp))
mshap <- data.frame(
  feature = colnames(S),
  low_severity = colMeans(S[y_ex %in% 0:1, , drop = FALSE]),
  high_severity = colMeans(S[y_ex %in% 5:6, , drop = FALSE])
)
mshap$rank_low <- rank(-mshap$low_severity)
mshap$rank_high <- rank(-mshap$high_severity)
mshap %>%
  mutate(across(c(low_severity, high_severity), ~ round(., 3))) %>%
  arrange(desc(high_severity)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

- For this mid-severity crop no single feature dominates, the largest push being
  -0.28 from the log green-to-red ratio.
- Those small contributions carry the prediction from a 3.05 baseline to 2.42,
  which rounds to 2 and lands one class below the truth, the off-by-one error the
  confusion matrix is full of.

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=5}

#| fig-height: 5

p_wf <- sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = wf_row) +
  labs(title = sprintf("SHAP waterfall for one score-%d CDA", y_ex[wf_row]))
p_wf
save_plot(p_wf, "seg_shap_waterfall.png", width = 8, height = 5)
```

## 10. Importance against univariate separability

Gini and SHAP both rank features by how much a fitted model leans on them, which
is not the same as how well a feature separates severity on its own. The
univariate measure is the mean adjacent-class AUC from
`10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction`: for each neighbouring score pair
(0-1, 1-2, and so on) the probability that a CDA from the higher score has the
larger feature value, averaged over the six pairs, where 0.5 is no separation.
Plotting one against the other shows whether the models are simply recovering the
univariate ranking or exploiting something a single feature cannot see.

- Both rankings track separability almost exactly, at Spearman 0.95 for Gini and
  0.94 for SHAP, so neither model is finding much beyond what each feature
  already does on its own.
- `mean_green` is the clearest exception, separating adjacent classes at AUC 0.63
  yet drawing a mean absolute SHAP of only 0.07, because its signal is already
  carried by `cda_green` and `log_gr`, which it correlates with strongly.
- `cda_green_sd` sits at AUC 0.49 with the lowest score on both measures, so the
  models agree with the univariate view that lesion mottling is uninformative.

```{r fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
# 10.1  Mean adjacent-class AUC per feature, recomputed here from the exported
# table so this analysis stays self-contained. Definition matches
# 10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction, and it is measured on the full
# unbalanced dataset, since separability is a property of the feature rather
# than of the balanced sample the models are fitted on.
auc_pair <- function(hi, lo) {
  r <- rank(c(hi, lo))
  (sum(r[seq_along(hi)]) - length(hi) * (length(hi) + 1) / 2) /
    (length(hi) * length(lo))
}
adjacent_auc <- function(x, score) {
  ok <- is.finite(x)
  x <- x[ok]
  score <- score[ok]
  cls <- sort(unique(score))
  mean(vapply(seq_len(length(cls) - 1), function(k) {
    auc_pair(x[score == cls[k + 1]], x[score == cls[k]])
  }, numeric(1)))
}

# One scalar per feature for each importance measure: mean decrease in Gini from
# the classifier, and mean |SHAP| over the explanation set.
imp_cmp <- data.frame(
  feature = all_features,
  adj_auc = vapply(all_features, function(v) adjacent_auc(features[[v]], features$score), numeric(1)),
  gini = imp_df$importance[match(all_features, imp_df$feature)],
  mean_abs_shap = colMeans(abs(get_shap_values(shp)))[all_features]
)

imp_panel <- function(yvar, ylab, title) {
  rho <- cor(imp_cmp$adj_auc, imp_cmp[[yvar]], method = "spearman")
  ggplot(imp_cmp, aes(adj_auc, .data[[yvar]])) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(colour = "#2166AC", size = 2.4) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = feature), size = 3.1, max.overlaps = 20) +
    labs(
      x = "Mean adjacent-class AUC (0.5 = no separation)", y = ylab,
      title = sprintf("%s (Spearman rho = %.2f)", title, rho)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11), axis.title = element_text(size = 12))
}
p_imp_cmp <- imp_panel("gini", "Mean decrease in Gini", "Gini importance") |
  imp_panel("mean_abs_shap", "Mean |SHAP|", "SHAP importance")
p_imp_cmp
save_plot(p_imp_cmp, "seg_importance_vs_separability.png", width = 11, height = 5)

cat(sprintf(
  "Spearman vs adjacent-class AUC:  Gini = %.3f  |  mean |SHAP| = %.3f\n",
  cor(imp_cmp$adj_auc, imp_cmp$gini, method = "spearman"),
  cor(imp_cmp$adj_auc, imp_cmp$mean_abs_shap, method = "spearman")
))
print(imp_cmp[order(-imp_cmp$adj_auc), ], row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
```

---

## 11. Interpretation and Discussion

- The features place a CDA within one point of its score almost always but pin
  the exact score only about 60% of the time. Ordinal regression averages 60.8%
  exact across 1,000 balanced undersamples (95% interval 59.7 to 61.9) and 97.7%
  near-miss, so the ordering is recoverable while the exact class is not.
- A linear model on an ordered scale is enough, and the margin is real. Ordinal
  regression beats the random forest (56.5%) and k-NN (55.6%) with only twelve
  coefficients and six cut-points, and every one of the 1,000 undersamples clears
  both, so there is little non-linear structure left for a tree ensemble to find.
- Single-undersample figures should be read with care. The seed-42 draw reports
  61.5% exact, the 91st percentile of the resampled distribution, so any headline
  resting on one balanced sample can be a point optimistic.
- Regularising the forest costs almost nothing. A fully grown forest hits 92.4%
  training accuracy against 57.0% held-out, and capping it at 128 leaf nodes
  gives up 0.8 points of held-out accuracy to close a 35-point gap.
- Gini importance and SHAP agree on what matters. CDA greenness and the log
  green-to-red ratio lead both rankings, while the two within-CDA texture
  features contribute a mean absolute SHAP of 0.01, so how mottled a lesion is
  matters far less than how green and bright it is.
- Grouping folds by leaf changes less than expected. It costs the fully grown
  forest 1.9 points and the regularised forest 0.9, and leaves ordinal regression
  unchanged at 61.5% against 60.9% ungrouped, so the headline result was never
  resting on leaked leaf identity.
- Low scores remain hard. Every interior class sits near 55% exact against 79.8%
  at score 0, so mild cell death is genuinely close to healthy tissue and to its
  neighbours, which is why a learned model is needed for the fine-grained scores.
